name: Agarikodaio
story:
Its shape is the work of axes. For generations charcoal burners in the Nakajimadai forest cut this beech off above the winter snowpack, and each cut sent up a new crop of stems from the same living base. In local dialect a tree treated that way is an agariko, a risen-up child. This one is the daio, the king of them: a squat trunk 7.62 metres round splitting into a candelabra of limbs that reach 25 metres.

Japan's Forestry Agency surveyed it, listed it among its hundred Forest Giants and dates it at over three hundred years. Nobody has cut it in a very long time, and the stems left standing at that last cut have had generations to thicken into trunks of their own.

This is not a temple tree or a shrine tree, which is how most old trees in Japan came through the centuries. It is a working tree that outlived its work. The beech woods around it were fuel, and the deep snow that decided where the woodsmen swung their axes still buries the ground here for months.

It stands in Chokai Quasi-National Park, reached on a marked forest path from the Nakajimadai trailhead, and it is now one of the most photographed trees in northern Japan. In leaf, the candelabra vanishes into its own canopy. Before the leaves come, you can read the whole strange frame of it.
access: Free, reached via a marked forest trail in Nakajimadai within Chokai Quasi-National Park
transport: No train station nearby; reached by car to the Nakajimadai trailhead near Kisakata, then a short walk on the marked forest path

name: Aizen Katsura
age_estimate: several hundred years (sources disagree, from 300 to over 1,000)

location.address: Kitamuki Kannon precinct, Bessho Onsen, Ueda, Nagano Prefecture

story:
A novel and a film were named after this tree. Kawaguchi Matsutaro's Aizen Katsura came out in 1938 and reached the screen the same year, and the katsura behind the title stands in the grounds of Kitamuki Kannon at Bessho Onsen. Its leaves are heart-shaped, said to bring luck in love, which is why couples still walk up to it.

The official recognition came a year after the novel. Nagano Prefecture listed the tree as a natural monument in 1939, and the city of Ueda re-listed it as one of its own in 1974. It reaches 22 metres on a trunk 5.8 metres round, breaking upward into the crowd of vertical stems that old katsura grow instead of one clean bole.

Its age is a genuine argument. Published estimates run at over 300 years, at 600 to 650, at over 1,000 and at about 1,200, and none of them arrives with a measurement attached. Several hundred years is the part every source agrees on. Beyond that, the number you get depends on who is telling you.

The tree stands out in the open in the temple grounds rather than behind anything, free to anyone who gets there in daylight, about a quarter of an hour on foot up from Bessho Onsen station. If you know what actually dates it, tell us.
access: Free, stands in the grounds of Kitamuki Kannon temple, open to visitors during daylight hours
transport: Ueda Dentetsu Bessho Line to Bessho Onsen Station, then about 10-15 minute walk to Kitamuki Kannon

name: Akatsu no Katsura
story:
Japan made this katsura a national natural monument on 27 January 1941, and it has been getting smaller ever since. The record made at the designation describes a tree over 30 metres tall with a crown spreading about as wide. Typhoons have taken limbs since then and soil has washed out from under its roots, leaving 25 metres of height and a 20 metre spread. It is still one of the largest katsura in the country.

The trunk measures 3.5 metres through at chest height, and at roughly 1.2 metres above the ground it stops pretending to be a single tree: fourteen stems, some huge and some slight, climb out of it from that point. Old katsura routinely do this. Very few do it on this scale.

That 1941 survey is also the only reason anyone can say what the tree has lost. Its age is put at over 350 years, with nothing published about what the figure rests on, so read three and a half centuries as a floor rather than a verdict. If you know what dates it, tell us.

It stands unfenced on a rural road toward Aizu-Nunobikiyama, west of Koriyama, with no station within reach. Our coordinates mark the area rather than the trunk, so expect a short hunt when you arrive.
access: Free, standing beside a rural road/trail area, publicly viewable
transport: No nearby train station; reached by car, roughly 8km from Konan-machi Akatsu toward Aizu-Nunobikiyama

name: Hagurosan no Jiji Sugi

location.address: Sando approach path, Mt Haguro (Hagurosan), Tsuruoka, Yamagata Prefecture

story:
This tree used to be half of a couple. Baba Sugi, the grandmother cedar, stood beside it until a storm brought her down in 1902, and Jiji Sugi, the grandfather, has kept the spot alone ever since.

He is the oldest and the largest tree on Mt Haguro: put at over a thousand years, 43 metres tall, a trunk 8.25 metres round, and roots flaring to a girth of 10.5 metres where they take hold of the slope. That distinction matters here, because Mt Haguro is covered in old cedars. The avenue lining the stone stairway, the Sugi Namiki, is famous in its own right, and this trunk is older and thicker than any tree in it. Walk past quickly and you take it for the best specimen in the row. It is a separately named tree with its own designation and its own history.

It stands directly beside the sando, the pilgrimage path climbing from the Zuishinmon gate to the summit shrine of the Dewa Sanzan, so everyone working up the steps passes within a few metres of it. Nobody has to leave the path or pay anything to stand at the base.

The bus from Tsuruoka Station stops at Zuishinmon-mae. From there it is stone steps under cedar shade, and the grandfather waits partway up.
access: Free, stands directly beside the public sando (pilgrimage path) between the Zuishinmon gate and the summit of Mt Haguro
transport: Bus from Tsuruoka Station to the Haguro Zuishinmon-mae stop, then on foot up the stone-step sando; the tree stands partway up
